title: Given a list of points on a plane and a value K, find the K points closest to the origin. Explain how a max-heap keyed on squared distance keeps the K nearest and why squared distance avoids the square root.
shortTitle: K Closest Points to the Origin (Nearest K Points by Distance)

s1_definition.profdef: K Closest Points to the Origin is a Top K Elements problem. We keep a max-heap of size K ordered by distance from the origin, where the root is the farthest of the kept points. Each new point replaces the root only if it is closer. We compare by squared distance to avoid the cost and precision loss of the square root, since ordering is preserved. This gives O(n log K) time.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, each branch is a point on a map and we want the K branches nearest to head office at the origin. We keep a small bucket of the K nearest branches, with the farthest of them on top. A new branch enters only if it is nearer than that farthest one. We rank by distance-squared because taking actual distances with a square root is unnecessary for ordering.
s1_definition.oneliner: Max-heap of size K by squared distance; a closer point evicts the farthest kept point.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** K Closest Points to the Origin is a Top K Elements problem. We keep a max-heap of size K ordered by distance from the origin, where the root is the farthest of the kept points. Each new point replaces the root only if it is closer. We compare by squared distance to avoid the cost and precision loss of the square root, since ordering is preserved. This gives O(n log K) time.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, each branch is a point on a map and we want the K branches nearest to head office at the origin. We keep a small bucket of the K nearest branches, with the farthest of them on top. A new branch enters only if it is nearer than that farthest one. We rank by distance-squared because taking actual distances with a square root is unnecessary for ordering.

**One line to remember:** Max-heap of size K by squared distance; a closer point evicts the farthest kept point.

sections.s2_technical:
For a point with coordinates x and y, the squared distance from the origin is x times x plus y times y. We never need the actual Euclidean distance because comparing squared distances gives the same ordering, and it avoids a floating-point square root. We build a max-heap keyed on that squared distance: `PriorityQueue<int[]> maxHeap = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> (b[0]*b[0] + b[1]*b[1]) - (a[0]*a[0] + a[1]*a[1]));`.

We push the first K points, then for each remaining point we compare its squared distance with the root's squared distance, which is the farthest kept; if the new point is closer we poll and offer. At the end the heap holds the K closest points. Keeping the farthest at the root makes the keep-or-discard decision a single comparison.

A senior nuance is the squared-distance optimisation, which both saves the square-root computation and avoids floating-point rounding issues by staying in integer arithmetic when coordinates are integers. Another nuance is that for a static array quickselect on squared distance gives average linear time, but the heap shines for streaming points. Complexity is O(n log K) time and O(K) space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India plots branches as coordinates and wants the K branches nearest to head office at the origin, for a cash-logistics route, without sorting all branches. This is exactly how K Closest Points works.

Problem 2 — Computing exact distances with square roots for every branch and sorting them is wasteful and imprecise. This is why we keep a max-heap of size K keyed on squared distance, evicting the farthest kept branch when a nearer one appears.

The code defines a `BranchLocatorService` exposing `kClosest(points, k)` returning the K nearest branch coordinates. A `Demo` finds the two nearest branches and logs them.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: branches at coordinates one-three, minus-two-two, five-eight, zero-one and K equal to 2.

Step 1: Squared distances are: one-three gives 1 plus 9 equals 10; minus-two-two gives 4 plus 4 equals 8; five-eight gives 25 plus 64 equals 89; zero-one gives 0 plus 1 equals 1.

Step 2: Seed the max-heap with the first two points, one-three with 10 and minus-two-two with 8; the root is one-three with the larger distance 10.

Step 3: Next point five-eight has distance 89, which is not less than root 10, so ignore it.

Step 4: Next point zero-one has distance 1, which is less than root 10, so pop one-three and push zero-one; the heap now holds minus-two-two with 8 and zero-one with 1.

Step 5: The two nearest branches are minus-two-two and zero-one.


sections.s6_takeaway:
K Closest Points to the Origin is a Top K Elements problem where I want the K nearest points, so I keep a max-heap of size K ordered by distance. Because it is a max-heap, its root is the farthest of the points I am currently keeping, which makes the keep-or-discard decision for each new point a single comparison: if the new point is closer than the farthest kept point, I evict the root and insert the new point.

An important optimisation is that I rank points by squared distance, x times x plus y times y, rather than true Euclidean distance. Squared distance preserves the same ordering, so it gives identical results while avoiding the cost of a square root and, when coordinates are integers, avoiding floating-point rounding entirely by staying in integer arithmetic. That is a small but telling detail of numerical care.

At the National Bank of India I used this to find the K branches nearest head office, modelled at the origin, for planning a cash-logistics route, without sorting all branches. I kept a size-K max-heap keyed on squared distance so each nearer branch evicted the farthest kept one, running in n log K time. Explaining the max-heap-for-nearest choice and the squared-distance trick is what shows an interviewer I combine the right structure with numerically clean comparisons.
